初學先以坐姿將琴置於腿上，琴頸直立；站姿則以胯部夾持琴身取得支撐，琴頸垂直朝上。: To begin, sit with the instrument on your legs and the neck upright; standing, grip the body with the hips for support and keep the neck vertical. Sound it mainly by plucking and strumming, chiefly with the thumb and index finger and occasionally with the middle finger; the strings are fixed to an upright bridge and wound round the neck, with a square wooden box for resonance. In practice, first hold the instrument steadily, then sound it by plucking with the thumb or index finger, then practise strumming, and finally add dance or movement.

塞佩雷瓦琴擁有溫潤而富有穿透力的音色，具有明亮的高頻特性與深沉的低頻共鳴。其音域: The seperewa has a warm, penetrating timbre, with bright high frequencies and deep low resonance. Its range is wide, spanning the middle-low to the high register, and it can produce rich layers of tone. The resonance of the vibrating strings has a distinctive metallic quality with a slight nasal edge; the tone is neither too sharp nor too dark. Beside the Mandinka kora the seperewa sounds warmer and fuller; beside the Sisala koridu its sound carries further. The structure of the body gives the resonance a natural decay, which suits narrative melody; the tone has a strong folk character and can convey the deep cultural content of traditional African music.
塞佩雷瓦琴琴身主要由非洲硬木製成，通常採用當地優質的共鳴木材如紅木或相思木。琴頸: The body of the seperewa is made mainly from African hardwood, usually a good local resonant timber such as mahogany or acacia. The neck and the post are of hard, durable wood. The strings are traditionally of animal gut, with excellent resonance. The resonating chamber inside the body may be lined with animal leather or plant fibre to strengthen the sound. Some decorative parts may use shell, bone or wooden beads. The whole design makes full use of the acoustic properties of natural materials.

In the early twentieth century, as the Akan kingdoms were absorbed into the Gold Coast colony and Christianity spread, the instrument entered churches, Christian weddings and meetings. It can be played solo or with singing; the player can sit with the instrument on the knees or stand gripping the body, plucking or strumming with thumb and index finger, and can dance while playing. Similar harp-lutes were once widespread in northern Ghana and were later largely replaced by gourd lutes such as the kologo and molo, surviving only among the southern Akan; there is also the six-string koriduo of the Dagari and Sisala in the northwest. Opoku Ware, successor of the Ashanti king Osei Tutu, had a copy covered in gold leaf made and placed among the objects of the Golden Stool. British colonisation in the later nineteenth century and the arrival of the guitar made it decline; in the early twentieth century it entered churches, Christian weddings and meetings.

The seperewa (also seprewa or sanku) is the traditional harp-lute of the Akan people of Ghana, a West African harp-lute chordophone with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 323-5. Its soundbox is usually a square wooden box, and modern instruments commonly have 10 to 14 strings, fixed to an upright bridge and wound directly round the neck. The player uses mainly the thumb, occasionally the index or middle finger, and can sit with the instrument on the legs or stand gripping the body, sounding it by plucking and strumming. In the past it was used to entertain kings, in palm-wine bars and at funerals, and since the early twentieth century it has also entered churches, Christian weddings and meetings.
